content:
Discussing with @Paul Reichert, I have realized that there is a question I have on the current Lean design, where Lean is doing something and I don't know if it's the "correct" behavior, or what the correct behavior should be.

The question is the following: suppose that, to some object a is attached some typeclass, and that there is a rfl simp lemma that would rewrite a to b -- but b doesn't have the same typeclass as a (think a is a type synonym for b, or a is some functor composition and b changes the associativity). What should happen when we rewrite or simp a to b: should
(1) the instance be ported to b (but then b gets an instance which is not the one that would be found by typeclass inference)
(2) the instance not be ported to b, so we get a term which is weird, with b but the instance of a
(3) rw and simp complain and fail

Currently, Lean does (2) if I understand correctly. MWE:

def myCopy (n : Nat) : Nat := n
def myCopy2 (n : Nat) : Nat := n

theorem myCopy_eq_myCopy2 (n : Nat) : myCopy n = myCopy2 n := rfl

class myClass (n : Nat) where
  new : Nat

instance instMyClassMyCopy (n : Nat) : myClass (myCopy n) where
  new := n

instance instMyClassMyCopy2 (n : Nat) : myClass (myCopy2 n) where
  new := 2 * n

def foo (n : Nat) [hn : myClass n] : Nat := hn.new

theorem foo_myCopy2_eq (n : Nat) : foo (myCopy2 n) = 2 * n := rfl

theorem foo_eq (n : Nat) : foo_myCopy_eq (myCopy n) = 2 * n := by
  -- rw [myCopy_eq_myCopy2]  -- fails with `motive not type correct` error as I would expect
  simp [myCopy_eq_myCopy2]
  -- works, and creates a term @foo (myCopy2 n) (instMyClassMyCopy n)
  -- this looks bad as myCopy2 has an instance, and it's not that one!
  -- goal in the infoview looks like `foo (myCopy2 n) = 2 * n`
  apply foo_myCopy2_eq -- fails, of course but confusingly

The question is: should we do (3) instead, i.e., should simp fail in this situation? And the meta-question: is that a good design to rewrite or simp things that carry some instances, if the rewritten or simped stuff wouldn't carry the same instance? I don't expect this to happen in typical situations I am familiar with, but maybe that's something that's very convenient in category theory, say.

Comment most welcome!

Yes, I can confirm that Lean is doing (2). simp won't do such a rewrite, but dsimp will, because in theory, definitional rewrites can't produce an ill-typed term. (That reasoning obviously ignores transparency.)

Here's an addition to the design space: Usually in such situtions, we are talking about [instance-implicit] arguments. However, there are legitimate reasons to have instances in {implicit} arguments, like {_ : Ord a}, when we expect the instance to be unified by the LHS of a simp lemma, for example. The question then is whether we also count this as an instance whose coherence we care about.

This can be relevant when an application of f (x) {_ : InstanceDependingOn x} gets unfolded to an application of g (x) [InstanceDependingOn x]. If incoherence for {_ : InstanceDependingOn x} is allowed, unfolding will again produce an incoherent instance inside [InstanceDependingOn x] of the g application.

I think docs#associatesNonZeroDivisorsEquiv is an in-the-wild case: we define a MulEquiv using an existing Equiv on Quotients, taking advantage of the fact that Associates is a Quotient, but unfolding Associates means it loses its Mul instance. Replacing the repeat rw with simp fails.
Do we have any stats on the breakage of (3)?

I tried this a few weeks ago (only for [instance-implicit] arguments) and was aghast from its consequences -- lots of failures and fragility. But @Sébastien Gouëzel convincend me to take a look again and provide some real data.

This would amount to nerfing simp, making dsimp less powerful. If I remember correctly, there were some comments by @Joël Riou and @Robin Carlier that it would be a big loss for category theory, but maybe they can explain better.
A qualification: dsimp rewriting at instance transparency is no problem, only rewrites that don't hold at instance transparency are an issue, but still. I'll come back when I have something to show
Yes, precisely. If we see breakage in mathlib, it might be a symptom that more things should be abbrevs (if we expect them to hold the same instances after simplification).

I do not know how much of failures of 3. we would have in category theory. Hopefully, it should not be a big issue in the most recent polished/clean-up code that does not use set_option (typically by making lots of things implicit_reducible defs [and abbrevs would be ok when there are no issues with instance inference]). (There are still more than 2300 set_option ... respectTransparency... false in category theory.)

implicit_reducible doesn't help with the instance-coherence problem we're discussing: If I rewrite x to y and x =?= y holds at implicit but not instance transparency, then i : Class x, which might still be lying around in the term, suddenly sits in a position expecting Class y, even though i is not a valid instance for Class y, because it has the wrong type (at instance transparency).
This is what makes it such a delicate issue: The usual advice that rfl lemmas are legitimate if their equality holds at implicit transparency doesn't prevent it.

I’m also not sure about how much (3) would break in category theory unless it is tried. I don’t think we rely that much on this mechanism, so breakages would probably just highlight cases of genuine abuse.
The main place I can think of where this could have been a problem is in the variations of comma categories that we have (over/under categories, arrows, structured arrows, etc.), but in April @Joël Riou introduced some API separation, so hopefully this will be fine.

I tried it out here, mechanically adding backward options to all failures. There are still >100 modules blocked by errors that can't be resolved mechanically, perhaps due to simps-generated lemmas from further upstream that are looking different now (I don't know).

https://github.com/leanprover/downstream-lean4/pull/68

This is a fairly complex solution.

  • It doesn't apply to propositional type classes. This is probably right in 99% of all cases, but there are conceivable use cases where this is unintended.
  • If an instance's type becomes incoherent through the application of a rfl lemma, Lean tries to re-synthesize the instance, and then ensures that the synthesized instance is defeq (at implicit) to the old one. This recovery mechanism makes it less fragile.
  • It doesn't apply to {implicit} instance arguments. That's something I simply haven't tried.

The tests in your PR look very nice!

I can try to have a look at some of the Mathlib failure, but for that I would need some instructions for newbies on how to get the branch and its cache on my computer -- because if I see correctly this is not on Mathlib or one of its forks, so my standard workflow doesn't work here.

Yes -- there's a new mechanism for testing downstream libraries with toolchain changes. The following should work.

  • Clone that repository and check out the branch of the PR.
  • Run .meta/get-cache.sh mathlib4.
  • cd into mathlib4 and run lake build.

You should be able to open the cloned repository in VSCode and edit the files there. The branch contains two changes to Batteries and ~200 to Mathlib. If you're on macOS, chances are that the toolchain isn't available yet. I can add the merge-CI label to the lean4 repo in order to make it available.

I haven't tested how much work would be needed on top of this to fix lean4#14949 yet (i.e. how much else still breaks after enabling respectTransparency.instances, which is the option that adds stricter checks whenever we assign an instance metavariable). There are still many failure modes, like the resynthesization being too slow or the need to consider {implicit} arguments. But I think it's good to get a feeling for the consequences of this change.
Independently of lean4#14949, I think it would be good to get this into Lean, because the dsimp magic not playing nice with transparency is just bad. Thanks for the instructions, let me have a look!

Is there a way to whitelist things for which we would be ready to get wrong instances? I am thinking of DecidableEq or DecidableLE, which show up quite often in the warnings and shouldn't be problematic.

Yes, there is: The class needs the @[lax_instance_defeq] attribute for that. (In the case of DecidableLE I guess Decidable would need that.)

As a subsingleton, whitelisting Decidable is unproblematic sematically, although one would then still be able to run into lean4#14949 issues around Decidable. It's not a defeq subsingleton. It's really a headache of a value-dependent type class.

I have a question on a random file in the PR, with a warning: in Mathlib.Analysis.Analytic.ChangeOrigin, line 168. The statement is about some element of E [×s.fst + s.snd.fst]→L[𝕜] F (whatever that is), i.e., a type that depends on the integers s.fst and s.snd and on an AddCommMonoid typeclass. The line has dsimp [changeOriginIndexEquiv_symm_apply_fst] which rewrites s.fst to something else, so we're exactly in the setting of the issue. The error message is

A rewrite with changeOriginIndexEquiv_symm_apply_snd_fst changed an argument of
  E [×(changeOriginIndexEquiv.symm x).fst + (changeOriginIndexEquiv.symm x).snd.fst]→L[𝕜] F
The instance argument
  fun i ↦ inst✝³.toAddCommMonoid
then does not have the expected type at `.instances` transparency, and no usable replacement instance was found. The rewrite was not applied here.

Here, when we rewrite, the new type should have an AddCommMonoid instance, and the new instance should be defeq to the original one if we ignore all transparencies issues. So I thought this was precisely the case were the dsimp should work. Am I missing something?
The problem seems to be inside of the i binder. The types of the binder would only match at default transparency. That might also be the reason why respectTransparency false is needed here.
So the underlying problem is that changeOriginIndexEquiv_symm_apply_fst violates the rule that rfl lemmas should hold at implicit transparency. This one doesn't.

Just for the record, the files that fail the build:

- Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Monoidal.Cartesian.Ring
- Mathlib.AlgebraicTopology.SimplicialSet.Homotopy
- Mathlib.AlgebraicTopology.SimplicialSet.AnodyneExtensions.UnionProd
- Mathlib.Topology.Sheaves.LocalPredicate
- Mathlib.RepresentationTheory.Homological.GroupHomology.LowDegree

Interestingly, not a single additional error appears if we also do this check for {implicit} class-typed arguments.

What I still don't like about this solution is that it makes (d)simp even less predictable. It already got a bit less predictable with respectTransparency true. Currently, my implementation shows a warning when a lemma is suppressed, but we don't want these warnings in production: lemmas can be suppressed rightfully in a dsimp, and getting rid of the warning would force the user to somehow exclude that lemma. But without the warning, the user won't notice when a lemma doesn't trigger that, for example, is necessary for confluence or for simps to reach the correct normal form.

I still think it would make sense to have a simp set of theorems that dsimp uses under backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward true. And we could have simps automatically add its generated theorems to this simp set. A previously suggested name for this simp set and acompanying tactic is rfl_simp. Then we could replace many uses of dsimp with rfl_simp.

However, I haven't tried this, so I don't actually know how many of the over 4000 backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward true we can remove like this.

I think I don't understand what such a simp set would buy. Why would auto-generated lemmas land in that simp set? Which problem would that address?

The problem I was trying to express above is that simps uses simp while determining the statement of the generating lemmas. If simp silently suppresses a lemma, then the resulting statement might be unexpected.

If I understand the idea behind rfl_simp correctly, it's like dsimp with useBackward true. What's the point behind introducing a new tactic that only differs in how it treats a backward compatibility annotation? That annotation will go away at some point.

The difference is that instead of using the backwards option, it is just a plain simp set. So it can still be used after the backwards option goes away. In particular, this means that the lemmas that don't hold in implicit_reducible will not be used in dependent arguments (which the backwards version of dsimp does do).

The idea then is that this simp set is stable enough that we can simplify with it, without needing to write the lemmas explicitly as in simp only.

Okay, I think I understand it now. Are you looking for a way to apply backward_defeq lemmas as normal simp lemmas, instead of dsimp lemmas, but as part of a more restricted simp set? So that rfl_simp would be allowed nonterminally in Mathlib while simp wouldn't be.
